did_you_know.text: Did you know? The prophecy begins in the land of Hadrach and Damascus, emphasizing that the LORD’s eye is focused on humanity and on all the tribes of Israel.
Did you know? Tyre is described as a heavily fortified and very wealthy city: it amassed silver like dust and gold like the mud in its streets.
Did you know? Despite its wealth and fortifications, Tyre is destined to be destroyed: the LORD will dispossess it, strike down its power in the sea, and the city will be consumed by fire.
Did you know? Tyre’s fall strikes fear into the cities of Philistia: Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron are described as losing their security, and the king of Gaza will disappear.

Did you know? The LORD describes a cleansing from idolatry and corrupt practices: the blood and detestable things will be removed, and the remnant of the Philistines will belong to the God of Israel and become like a clan leader in Judah.
Did you know? The LORD promises to protect his house from armies and oppressors, declaring that this time he has seen its situation with his own eyes.

Did you know? The future king who will come to Jerusalem is described as righteous, saved, and humble, riding on a donkey—on a colt, the foal of a donkey—a description that emphasizes his humility rather than military grandeur.

Did you know? The king’s rule is described as bringing peace: the weapons of war will be destroyed, he will proclaim peace to the nations, and his rule will extend from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.
Did you know? Because of the blood of the covenant, the LORD promises to free the prisoners from the waterless pit—a picture of deliverance from a hopeless situation.

Did you know? In the prophecy, Judah is compared to a bow and Ephraim to its arrow, while the people of Zion confront the people of Greece; thus the LORD is portrayed as strengthening his people for battle.
